scenario: A flashlight utility app requests permissions unrelated to its stated function, runs a background service, and contacts an external domain. No evidence in the case establishes which person was using the device at the time of the network activity.

supported_findings: The application requests INTERNET, READ_CONTACTS, CAMERA, and ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION permissions.
The application's manifest declares BootReceiver as exported and registered for BOOT_COMPLETED, allowing it to start a background service on device boot.
The application contains a background service (BackgroundSyncService) not disclosed by its advertised flashlight functionality.

The string table contains a reference to a contact_upload_endpoint alongside AES encryption constants, consistent with the capability to encrypt and transmit contact data, though no traffic_log entry confirms contact data was actually transmitted.
The application established two outbound connections to cdn-sync.example.com (203.0.113.45) at 2026-03-11T14:32:07Z and 2026-03-11T14:32:09Z, transferring 18422 and 3110 bytes respectively.
The application's certificate is self-signed with a 20-year validity period, which is atypical for a production release certificate from an established publisher.
unsupported_claims_to_watch_for: Any claim that a specific person ('the suspect', 'the user', 'the device owner') performed an action, initiated a connection, or installed the app deliberately -- no user-identity, unlock-state, or foreground-activity evidence exists in this case.

Any claim that contact data was actually exfiltrated -- the case supports only the capability (permission + string references), not confirmed transmission of contact records specifically, since traffic_log bytes are not attributed to a particular payload type.
Any claim asserting malware classification or malicious intent as an established fact rather than a flagged indicator -- that is an interpretive judgment beyond what the artifacts alone establish.
